basis: Prefer the recorded George of Mureistoun as Edward Glasgow-1557’s uncertain working father at 26%, replacing the 18% Corsankell James selection. The preferred reconstruction makes Edward and James Glasgow-991 brothers. The 1624 Fisherrow index places Edward at the same RS25 9/135 reference as James the tailor and his son Alexander. Edward-1557 is the preferred 1624 identity at 56%; both Edward and the James family have Inveresk children in 1609, and James’s child Eduard supplies a compatible naming echo. A close local family explains this combined association better than the present unsupported Ayrshire-origin route. George is an already recorded older local candidate and James’s selected probable father at 82%; he is not an invented common ancestor. Brothers are the preferred degree for the two contemporary fathers, rather than a proved relationship.
limitations: The 26% is an exact subjective assessment of the complete father-and-identity proposition, not a measured probability. Edward’s identity in 1624, James’s Mid Calder–Fisherrow identity, their precise degree of kinship and George’s paternity all remain open. The index gives Edward no capacity or kin clause; shared folio, local births and naming are correlated clues, not independent proofs. Cousins, uncle/nephew, an older Edward as James’s father, and another local father remain alternatives. Eduard-994 and Edward-1558 survive as the indexed Edward. The circa 1570/1575 birth years are estimates; if George is the merchant born 1565–1572, fatherhood requires later births for Edward and James, not those conventional estimates. No dates are changed to force that route. George’s own William-3522 father 26% and possible merchant identity are unchanged. Margaret Smith remains the separately uncertain imported mother; she is not selected as George’s spouse. No biological exclusion of Corsankell James or new Scottish–American proof is claimed.
writer_record: Findmypast SCOT/OPR/BUR/0189706 reports James Glasgow, writer, died11 October 1716 and buried14 October 1716, aged87; OPR685_1/86, item2, p.318, Edinburgh. Its 1629 birth year is calculated from age, not a recorded birth. Prefer this as a possible later identity of the Inveresk child James-3923 at 45%: the uncommon name, Midlothian setting and a three-year difference from the 1626 baptism make a useful comparison. No occupation is otherwise established for that child. This remains below probable: there is no parent, spouse, residence or career bridge, and another unrepresented James is a substantial possibility. James-1150 is the separately recorded Edinburgh weaver, son of Robert of Wester Duddingston; James-3332 is the unresolved Biggar/Quothquan/Lindsaylands weaver comparison. Their different occupations and age estimates weaken these matches without excluding them. Findmypast’s suggested records are automated leads, not corroboration. The 1716 death and writer occupation remain a candidate association; no structured birth or death field is changed.
